bplusTree.title: B+ Tree Index — Lookup, Insert & Node Split Mechanics
bplusTree.subtitle: Visualize why B+ trees maintain O(log N) lookup and how node splits propagate in relational databases like PostgreSQL (B-Tree) and MySQL InnoDB (Clustered Index).
bplusTree.mentalModel: A B+ tree keeps data sorted and balanced so any lookup is O(log N) — internal nodes route queries using keys, while all actual data/pointers reside in linked leaf nodes.

failureModes: Index Bloat: Frequent random inserts/deletes cause page splits and fragmentation, wasting memory and disk page reads.
Unindexed Sequential Scans: Missing appropriate composite indexes forces MySQL/Postgres to fall back to a full table scan ($O(N)$ disk I/O).
High Cardinality Index Overhead: Creating indexes on columns with continuous updates (e.g. timestamps or UUID v4) degrades insert throughput due to non-stop page splitting.
tradeOffs: B-Tree vs B+ Tree: B+ Trees store data pointers exclusively in leaves, allowing higher fan-out (more keys per internal node) and fast sequential leaf scans via linked pointers.

B+ Tree vs LSM-Tree: B+ Trees offer faster read lookups ($O(\log N)$ in-place pages), while LSM-Trees (used in Cassandra/RocksDB) offer faster append-only write throughput at the cost of read amplification.
theoryData.productionScenario: A multi-tenant e-commerce database saw query latency spike from 4ms to 4.2 seconds during Flash Sale events. Diagnosing `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` revealed `Seq Scan` on `orders (tenant_id, status)` because the index was created as `(status, tenant_id)`. Re-ordering the composite index prefix to high-cardinality `tenant_id` first reduced disk page reads from 45,000 to 3 pages per query.
theoryData.codeSnippet:
-- PostgreSQL Composite B+ Tree Index Creation
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_status ON orders (tenant_id, status);

-- Inspect Query Execution Plan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE tenant_id = 'tenant_9821' AND status = 'PENDING';

/* Output:
 Index Scan using idx_orders_tenant_status on orders 
   (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=128) (actual time=0.031..0.034ms)
   Index Cond: ((tenant_id = 'tenant_9821'::text) AND (status = 'PENDING'::text))
*/

interviewQA.q: Why do relational databases use B+ Trees instead of Binary Search Trees (BST) or Red-Black Trees?
interviewQA.a: Disk block access is the main bottleneck. BSTs have a low branching factor (fan-out of 2), requiring $O(\log_2 N)$ disk seeks. A B+ Tree node matches the OS disk page size (4KB/16KB), giving a fan-out of 100+ keys per node, reducing tree height to 3 or 4 levels even for millions of rows.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a Clustered Index and a Secondary Non-Clustered Index?
interviewQA.a: In InnoDB (MySQL), the Clustered Index stores full table row data inside the leaves of the primary key B+ Tree. A Secondary Index leaf stores only the Primary Key value, requiring a second B+ tree lookup ('bookmark lookup') to fetch full row data unless covered by an index.

interviewQA.q: What is a Covered Query in B+ Tree indexing?
interviewQA.a: A query is 'covered' when all SELECT and WHERE columns exist directly inside the secondary index keys. The database answers the query directly from the index leaf without performing a secondary lookup to the clustered table data page.

quizData.question: Suppose a B+ Tree of order M = 4 has a leaf node containing 3 keys [10, 20, 30]. If we insert key 25, what happens to the leaf node?
quizData.answer: Inserting 25 makes 4 keys [10, 20, 25, 30], which exceeds maxKeys (M-1 = 3). The leaf splits into two leaves: Left leaf [10, 20] and Right leaf [25, 30]. The key 25 (first key of the right leaf) is promoted upward into the parent internal node.

quizData.question: Why are sequential random UUID v4 primary keys considered an anti-pattern for B+ Tree indexes in MySQL InnoDB?
quizData.answer: UUID v4 values are completely random, causing inserts to hit arbitrary page locations across the B+ tree. This triggers constant leaf node splits, page fragmentation, and heavy disk I/O thrashing compared to monotonically increasing AUTO_INCREMENT or TSID/ULID keys.

quizData.question: How many disk page lookups are required for a 3-level B+ Tree with a root, internal layer, and leaf layer?
quizData.answer: With a 3-level tree: 1 page read for Root + 1 page read for Internal Node + 1 page read for Leaf Node = 3 disk I/Os. If Root and Internal nodes are cached in memory (Buffer Pool), it requires only 1 physical disk read!
